This is one of my go-to moves in hotel rooms because it hits your hips, thoracic spine, and ankles all at once—everything that gets locked up on long flights.

Start on hands and knees with wrists under shoulders and knees under hips—think stable four-point base like landing gear
Inhale as you drop your belly and lift your chest and tailbone up—this is Cow position
Exhale as you round your spine, tuck your tailbone, and drop your head—this is Cat position
Move slowly between positions for 8-10 breaths, matching one breath to one movement
Keep your neck neutral—don't crank it up or down, let it follow your spine naturally
Perfect for pre-flight or post-layover to counter the compressed sitting posture from the cockpit or jumpseat
common_mistakes: Rushing through the movement without linking it to your breath cycle.
Keeping your neck locked in one position instead of letting it flow naturally with your spine.
Moving only from your lower back rather than articulating through your entire spine from tailbone to skull.
Holding tension in your shoulders and forcing the movement instead of letting it flow smoothly.
Forgetting to engage your core, which turns a controlled spinal wave into a sloppy collapse.
client_facing_instructions: Start on your hands and knees with your wrists under your shoulders and knees under your hips. As you breathe in, drop your belly toward the floor, lift your chest and chin up—that's your Cow position. As you breathe out, round your spine up toward the ceiling like an angry cat, tucking your chin to your chest. Flow between these two positions for 8-10 breaths, moving with your breath. This is one of the best things you can do in a hotel room after a long flight to decompress your spine and wake up your core.

coaching_points: Hold a single dumbbell vertically at chest height with both hands cupping the top end, elbows tucked in
Stand feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out, core braced like you're prepping for turbulence
Descend by pushing hips back and knees out, keeping chest up and weight in your heels
Drop until your elbows brush the inside of your knees while maintaining a neutral spine
Drive through your heels to stand, squeezing glutes at the top without hyperextending your back
client_facing_instructions: Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest height with both hands cupping the top end—like you're holding a goblet—and stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Keep your chest proud and elbows pointing down as you push your hips back and descend into a squat, aiming to get your elbows between your knees at the bottom. Drive through your whole foot to stand back up, squeezing your glutes at the top. This is one of my favorite movements for building strong, stable legs in small spaces—the weight at your chest naturally keeps your torso upright and teaches proper squat mechanics, which translates directly to moving cargo and staying injury-free on the job.
common_mistakes: Dropping the chest forward and losing that upright torso position—your elbows should stay inside your knees throughout the movement.
Not going deep enough—you want hip crease below knee level if mobility allows, that's where the real benefit lives.
Letting the knees cave inward instead of tracking over the toes, which puts unnecessary stress on the knee joint.
Rising onto the toes instead of keeping weight distributed through the full foot, especially the heels.
Rushing the tempo—control the descent and explode up, don't just bounce out of the bottom.

coaching_points: Hinge at the hips by pushing them back, not by squatting down—keep your chest up like you're closing the overhead bins
Maintain a slight knee bend throughout the movement, knees shouldn't travel forward
Keep the weights close to your legs, skimming your thighs and shins on the way down
Stop when you feel tension in your hamstrings, typically mid-shin level—don't force depth
Drive your hips forward to stand up, squeezing your glutes at the top like you're standing at attention
common_mistakes: Rounding the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Bending the knees too much, turning it into a squat rather than a hip hinge.
Dropping the weight too low past the point where they can maintain proper form.
Not pushing the hips back far enough, keeping weight in the toes instead of the heels.
Looking up or craning the neck instead of keeping it neutral with the spine.
client_facing_instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a water bottle, bag, or even just your fists at your thighs. Keep a slight bend in your knees and push your hips back like you're closing a car door with your backside—this is the key movement. Lower the weight down your thighs while keeping your back flat and chest proud, going only as far as you can maintain that neutral spine (usually mid-shin). Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to stand back up. Think hinge at the hips, not squat—you should feel this working the back of your legs and glutes, which are critical for handling long flights and heavy bags without tweaking your lower back.

coaching_points: Find a quiet corner away from the gym floor—this works better in your hotel room or crew rest area.
Sit upright with your feet flat on the floor and hands resting on your thighs, maintaining an alert but relaxed posture.
Inhale through your nose for a controlled 4-count, filling your lungs from bottom to top.
Hold your breath for 4 counts without tensing your shoulders or chest—stay relaxed.
Exhale slowly through your mouth for 4 counts, emptying your lungs completely.
Hold empty for 4 counts, then repeat the cycle for 5 minutes—use this pre-flight or before sleep to regulate your nervous system.
common_mistakes: Rushing the counts or making them uneven, especially shortening the exhale when stress levels are high.
Breathing into the chest and shoulders instead of using the diaphragm, which defeats the calming purpose.
Holding tension in the jaw, neck, or shoulders during the holds instead of staying relaxed.
Forcing the breath holds to the point of panic or air hunger, which activates stress rather than reducing it.
Practicing only when already stressed instead of building the skill during calm moments first.
client_facing_instructions: Find a quiet spot—even the back of the cabin works. Sit upright, close your eyes if you can, and breathe in through your nose for a count of four. Hold that breath for four counts, then exhale slowly through your mouth for four, and hold empty for another four. That's one cycle. Run through four to five rounds, and you'll notice your heart rate settle and your mind clear—perfect before a tough leg or after a stressful delay.

coaching_points: Sit upright or stand tall—maintain neutral spine like you're in the flight deck
Inhale through your nose for 4 seconds, filling your belly first then chest
Hold the breath at the top for 2-3 seconds without tensing your shoulders
Exhale slowly through your mouth for 6 seconds, emptying completely
Keep your jaw relaxed and shoulders down throughout each cycle
Focus on smooth, controlled breaths—this primes your system before training or helps reset after long sectors
common_mistakes: Rushing through the breath cycles without allowing full lung expansion or complete exhalation.
Breathing into the chest only instead of allowing the diaphragm to drop and the belly to expand.
Holding tension in the shoulders, neck, or jaw while trying to breathe deeply.
Taking rapid, forceful breaths that can cause lightheadedness instead of controlled, steady inhales and exhales.
Breathing through the mouth only instead of using nasal breathing for better oxygen exchange and nervous system regulation.
client_facing_instructions: Find a quiet spot—your hotel room works perfectly. Sit upright or stand tall, and place one hand on your chest, the other on your belly. Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of four, feeling your belly expand (not just your chest), then exhale through your mouth for a count of six. Repeat this five times, focusing on making each breath deeper and more controlled than the last. This is your reset button after a long flight or before a tough duty period—use it.

coaching_points: Plant one foot flat, knee bent 90 degrees, and extend the other leg straight out at hip height
Drive through your heel to lift hips until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knee
Keep your core tight and squeeze the working glute hard at the top—don't let hips rotate or drop
Lower with control for three seconds, barely touching down before the next rep
If you're wobbling, place hands wider on the floor for stability until you build balance
common_mistakes: Pushing through the toes instead of driving through the heel, which shifts the work away from the glutes.
Letting the hips rotate or drop to one side instead of keeping them level throughout the movement.
Hyperextending the lower back at the top by pushing too high instead of stopping when the body forms a straight line.
Rushing the tempo and using momentum instead of controlled, deliberate reps with a squeeze at the top.
Not keeping the non-working leg in a stable position, allowing it to swing or drift which throws off balance.
client_facing_instructions: Lie on your back with one knee bent, foot flat on the floor, and extend the other leg straight out. Drive through your planted heel to lift your hips up until you form a straight line from shoulders to knee, keeping that extended leg in line with your body. Squeeze your glute hard at the top—this is where the work happens. Lower with control and repeat on one side before switching. If you're in a hotel room, this is perfect: no equipment needed, low impact for your downstairs neighbors, and it keeps your hips strong for those long flights.

Keep your torso upright and chest proud—don't lean forward at the hips
Lower your back knee to hover just above the floor, aiming for 90-degree angles at both knees
Drive through your front heel to return to standing, engaging your glutes and core throughout
Control the descent for two counts, then power back up—no bouncing at the bottom
common_mistakes: Stepping back too short, which loads the front knee past the toes and creates shear force.
Letting the front knee collapse inward instead of tracking over the toes in the same line.
Rushing the movement and bouncing out of the bottom position instead of controlling the descent.
Leaning the torso too far forward, which shifts load away from the legs and strains the lower back.
Allowing the back knee to slam into the ground rather than lowering it with control.
client_facing_instructions: Start standing tall with feet hip-width apart, hands on your hips or by your sides. Step one leg straight back, dropping your back knee toward the ground until both knees form roughly 90-degree angles—your front knee should track over your ankle, not beyond your toes. Push through your front heel to drive yourself back up to standing, bringing your feet together again. That's one rep. Keep your chest up and core engaged throughout, and alternate legs or complete all reps on one side before switching—either way works great when you're training in a hotel room or crew rest area.

coaching_points: Elevate rear foot on a bench or sturdy chair, front foot planted two to three feet forward

client_facing_instructions: Stand about two feet in front of a chair or bench, holding a dumbbell in each hand. Place the top of your rear foot on the surface behind you—laces down works best. This one's a killer for single-leg strength and balance, which matters when you're hauling bags through terminals after a red-eye—start light and nail the form before you go heavy.

Your floating leg can extend in front for balance, and if you're wobbling, that's normal—use a wall for a light fingertip assist until your stability catches up. Nail 6-8 controlled reps per side, and remember: depth matters less than control when you're working in tight spaces.

Engage your core and lift your shoulder blades off the ground by contracting your abs, bringing your ribcage toward your pelvis while keeping your lower back pressed down. Exhale as you crunch up, pause for a second at the top feeling that contraction, then slowly lower back down with control. Keep the movement small and controlled—this isn't about how high you go, it's about quality contraction of those abdominal muscles, which matters for maintaining stability during those long flights and irregular schedules.

Engage your core and avoid swinging or kicking your legs to maintain position.
Hold for time, aiming for 10-30 seconds depending on your current strength level.
Lower yourself under control when you can no longer maintain chin height—don't just drop off the bar.

client_facing_instructions: Find a sturdy bar or doorframe pull-up bar at home or in the hotel gym. Keep your shoulders engaged and pulled down, not hunched up by your ears. Hold the end position for 2 seconds, then return and repeat 10 times per ankle

client_facing_instructions: Stand facing a wall about six inches away, feet hip-width apart. Keep that foot flat on the ground and drive your knee forward over your toes, trying to touch the wall with your knee without your heel lifting off the floor. If you can touch easily, step back a bit further and repeat—you're looking for that controlled stretch in your ankle and lower calf. Do 10-15 reps per side, and this is brilliant prep before any lower body work or just to maintain ankle mobility between flights.

coaching_points: Place the ball of your foot on a low step or weight plate, keeping your heel on the ground
Keep your knee tracking forward over your toes while maintaining heel contact with the floor
Drive your knee as far forward as possible without lifting your heel—aim for shin-to-wall proximity
Hold the end position for two seconds, feeling the stretch in your calf and front of ankle
Perform 10-12 slow, controlled repetitions per side between flights to combat cabin stiffness
If balance is tricky, lightly touch a wall—this is about ankle range, not stability testing
Find a sturdy door frame or pull-up bar—test it with bodyweight before committing to full reps
Keep shoulders down and back, initiating the pull from your lats not your arms
Pull elbows straight down toward your hips, imagine crushing a can under each armpit
Control the negative—take 3 seconds to return to start position for maximum benefit
Stop immediately if you feel shoulder pinching—adjust grip width or switch to inverted rows under a table
